CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right great toe pain and redness for two weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents with a two-week history of right great toe pain and redness that has significantly worsened over the past week. While attending a trade show convention last week, the pain was severe enough to prevent ambulation through the halls. He describes the pain as throbbing in nature with occasional sharp, stabbing quality, particularly with movement or prolonged walking. Patient denies a specific traumatic injury. The toe became red and warm to the touch, which prompted evaluation. Light pressure exacerbates the pain, including from bed sheets when lying in bed at night. He has adapted his gait to walk on his heels to minimize bending of the great toe. He reports taking ibuprofen twice daily without significant relief.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies gastrointestinal issues. Pain is associated with passive range of motion of the great toe. Pain significantly worse at night with light pressure.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history reported. Denies chronic medical conditions.

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen, 2 tablets daily.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient is employed and works on his feet daily. He is an avid cyclist who rode over 800 miles on trails in the past year. He uses a regular shoe while cycling and pedals with the back of his feet. He typically wears flip flops. He also enjoys fishing during current fishing season, with a preference for catching blue gill and crappie. Reports enjoying spicy Mexican food.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Examination of the right foot:
- Passive range of motion testing of the first metatarsophalangeal joint provokes pain
- Dorsiflexion produces pain but is more tolerable
- Plantarflexion at 10 degrees produces some pain; plantarflexion at 20 degrees produces increased pain
- Axial loading with medial-lateral motion produces pain with palpable grinding sensation
- Palpation medial to the great toe produces mild discomfort
- Palpation lateral to the first metatarsophalangeal joint produces significant pain
- Bone spur palpated on the dorsal surface of the first metatarsophalangeal joint

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot demonstrates a large bone spur on the dorsal surface of the first metatarsophalangeal joint with significant cartilage loss.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hallux rigidus with osteoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

Plan:
1. Orthotic shoe insert for biomechanical support
2. Meloxicam (NSAID) once daily—generally well tolerated; patient counseled regarding potential gastric irritation and instructed to discontinue and call if heartburn or substernal pain develops
3. Continue regular work and daily activities to assess treatment effectiveness
4. Follow-up appointment in 2 weeks to reassess response to conservative management
5. If inadequate improvement with conservative measures, will consider more invasive interventions including intra-articular steroid injection, arthroscopic joint debridement, or first metatarsophalangeal joint fusion

Patient counseled to continue normal activities and work. Follow-up scheduled for two weeks.
